_note: Remedy records. MOST are `unverified`: the legacy dataset gave only a name and a condition pairing, and nothing further has been sourced. summary.value: The seeds of fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum), used as a food and traditional remedy.

traditionalUse.value: Traditionally used to support milk production during breastfeeding and, in some traditions, to help manage blood sugar and menstrual cramps.

contraindications.detail: Not considered safe during pregnancy in amounts greater than those found in food.

precautions.value: Can cause allergic reactions, including serious ones, particularly in people allergic to chickpeas or peanuts.
Large doses may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar, which matters if you have diabetes or take glucose-lowering medication.

interactions.value: May interact with medicines, including anticoagulants and diabetes medication — check with a healthcare professional first.

summary.value: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), a root used in Ayurvedic medicine, often as an adaptogen.

traditionalUse.value: Used for thousands of years in Ayurvedic medicine; currently promoted for stress, anxiety, sleep, and male fertility.

contraindications.detail: Should be avoided during pregnancy and not used while breastfeeding.
Not suitable for people with thyroid disorders or autoimmune conditions without medical advice.

precautions.value: May cause drowsiness, stomach upset, diarrhea, and vomiting.
Rare cases of liver injury have been reported. Safety is only established for short-term use (up to about three months).

summary.value: The rhizome of ginger (Zingiber officinale), used as a food and a traditional remedy.

traditionalUse.value: Traditionally used for indigestion and other gastrointestinal complaints; currently studied for nausea and vomiting, osteoarthritis, and menstrual cramps.

precautions.value: Can cause abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhea, and mouth or throat irritation when taken orally.
Talk to a healthcare provider before use if you take other medicines — some herb–medicine combinations interact in harmful ways.

interactions.value: May affect bleeding risk; discuss with a professional if you take anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication.
interactions.note: Widely cautioned but not stated on the cited NCCIH page — treat as editorial pending a specific source.

summary.value: A combination of boswellia (Boswellia serrata, 'shallaki') resin and curcumin, the active compound of turmeric (Curcuma longa).

traditionalUse.value: Turmeric has historically been used for arthritis and abdominal pain across several traditional systems; boswellia is traditionally used for inflammatory joint complaints.

contraindications.detail: Turmeric supplements may be unsafe during pregnancy.

precautions.value: Liver damage has been reported in some people taking concentrated, high-bioavailability turmeric/curcumin formulations. Stop and seek care for fatigue, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine, or jaundice.
